stem: Use the laws of logarithms to answer each part.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(\log_{3} 81 - \log_{3}\dfrac{1}{9}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write \(2\log x + \log 5 - \log 10\) as a single logarithm.

idea: \(\log a + \log b = \log ab\), \(\log a - \log b = \log\dfrac{a}{b}\) and \(n\log a = \log a^{n}\), in any base. A logarithm is defined only for positive numbers, so check every solution.

solution.label: c
steps: \((x + 8)(x - 2) = 0\). \(x = -8\) is rejected, because \(\log_{2}(-8)\) is not defined.

stem: Answer each part using the laws of exponents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve \(27^{x} = 9 \times 3^{x}\).

idea: A power \(\frac{p}{q}\) means the \(q\)th root, raised to the power \(p\). Writing both sides as powers of the same base turns an equation into an equation between the indices.

stem: The number of bacteria in a culture, \(N\), \(t\) hours after the start of an experiment is modelled by \(N = 500 \times 2^{\frac{t}{3}}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the initial number of bacteria and the time it takes for the number to double.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the number reaches 20 000 when \(t = \dfrac{3\log 40}{\log 2}\), and find this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second culture is modelled by \(M = 800 \times 1.15^{t}\). Find the time at which the two cultures have the same number of bacteria.

idea: To solve an equation with the unknown in the index, take logarithms of both sides: \(\log a^{x} = x\log a\). Change of base: \(\log_{2} 40 = \dfrac{\log 40}{\log 2}\).

solution.label: a
steps: At \(t = 0\), \(N = 500\). \(N\) doubles each time \(\dfrac{t}{3}\) increases by 1.

stem: This question is about logarithms in different bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(\log_{4} x = \dfrac{1}{2}\log_{2} x\) for \(x > 0\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence solve \(\log_{2} x + \log_{4} x = 6\).

idea: Write 1 as \(\log_{3} 3\) so that every term is a logarithm in base 3, then combine. Change of base: \(\log_{4} x = \dfrac{\log_{2} x}{\log_{2} 4}\).

stem: A geometric series is \(24 + 18 + 13.5 + \cdots\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the common ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the smallest number of terms for which the sum is more than 95.

idea: A geometric series with \(|r| < 1\) has a sum to infinity \(S_{\infty} = \dfrac{u_{1}}{1 - r}\). The partial sums get closer and closer to it.

stem: A recurring decimal can be written as an infinite geometric series.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(0.272727\ldots\) as an infinite geometric series, and hence show that it is equal to \(\dfrac{3}{11}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write \(0.4666\ldots\) as a fraction in its lowest terms.

idea: Split the decimal into its repeating blocks: each block is the previous one divided by a power of 10, so the blocks form a geometric series with \(|r| < 1\).

stem: A patient takes a 50 mg tablet every morning. By the next morning, 40 % of the amount of the drug in the body is still there; the rest has gone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the amount of the drug in the body just after the second tablet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the amount just after the fifth tablet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the amount just after a tablet in the long term.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the amount just before a tablet in the long term.

idea: Just after the \(n\)th tablet the body holds \(50 + 50(0.4) + 50(0.4)^{2} + \cdots + 50(0.4)^{n - 1}\): the newest tablet in full, and older ones reduced by 0.4 for each day. In the long term this is a sum to infinity.

stem: Consider the geometric series \(1 + (2x - 1) + (2x - 1)^{2} + (2x - 1)^{3} + \cdots\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the values of \(x\) for which the series has a sum to infinity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity in terms of \(x\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(x\) for which the sum to infinity is 4.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the sum to infinity cannot be 0.4.

idea: The common ratio is \(r = 2x - 1\), and a sum to infinity exists only when \(-1 < r < 1\). Then \(S_{\infty} = \dfrac{1}{1 - r}\).

solution.label: d
solution.answer: The sum to infinity is always more than 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(z + w\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(zw\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(|z|\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find \(\dfrac{z}{w}\) in the form \(a + bi\).

idea: Multiply out brackets as usual and use \(i^{2} = -1\). To divide, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which makes the denominator real.

stem: Consider the equation \(z^{2} + 4z + 13 = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the two solutions on an Argand diagram.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance between the two points on the Argand diagram.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the sum and the product of the two solutions.

idea: A quadratic with a negative discriminant has two complex solutions, which are conjugates of each other: mirror images in the real axis.

steps: Both points are on the line Re \(= -2\), from 3 to \(-3\).

stem: The complex number \(z = a + bi\), where \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\), satisfies \(z(2 - i) = 7 + 4i\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(a\) and \(b\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence write down both complex numbers whose square is \(-5 + 12i\).

idea: Divide by \(2 - i\) using the conjugate, or expand \((a + bi)(2 - i)\) and compare real and imaginary parts. If \(z^{2} = c\), then \((-z)^{2} = c\) too.

stem: Let \(z = 3 + 2i\). The points O, \(z\), \(z + iz\) and \(iz\) on an Argand diagram are the vertices of a quadrilateral, where O is the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(iz\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(|iz| = |z|\), and that the lines from O to \(z\) and from O to \(iz\) are perpendicular.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(z + iz\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence find the area of the quadrilateral.

idea: Multiplying by \(i\) rotates a point on the Argand diagram through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise about O, and keeps its distance from O. So O, \(z\), \(z + iz\) and \(iz\) form a square.

solution.label: b
steps: Gradient from O to \(z\): \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). Gradient from O to \(iz\): \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\). Their product is \(-1\).
solution.answer: Both have length \(\sqrt{13}\), and the gradients multiply to \(-1\)

solution.label: d
steps: Two equal perpendicular sides from O, with the fourth vertex \(z + iz\), make a square of side \(\sqrt{13}\).

stem: Let \(z = \dfrac{a + 3i}{2 - i}\), where \(a \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(z\) in the form \(x + yi\), where \(x\) and \(y\) are in terms of \(a\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\) for which \(z\) is real.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\) for which \(z\) is purely imaginary.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the values of \(a\) for which \(|z| = \sqrt{10}\).

idea: Make the denominator real with the conjugate \(2 + i\). Then \(z\) is real when its imaginary part is 0, and purely imaginary when its real part is 0.

stem: In this question, arguments are in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(z = -2 + 2\sqrt{3}\,i\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), where \(r > 0\) and \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write \(w = 3e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}i}\) in the form \(a + bi\), giving exact values.

idea: \(r = |z|\) and \(\theta = \arg z\), found from a sketch of the point. Going back: \(re^{i\theta} = r\cos\theta + ir\sin\theta\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(r = \sqrt{4 + 12} = 4\). The point is in the second quadrant: \(\theta = \pi - \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{2} = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

stem: Let \(z = 2e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}\) and \(w = 3e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(zw\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), and describe how multiplying \(z\) by \(w\) moves the point \(z\) on an Argand diagram.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write \(zw\) in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(\dfrac{z}{w}\) and \(z^{4}\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), where \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).

idea: In exponential form, multiply by multiplying the moduli and adding the arguments; divide by dividing the moduli and subtracting the arguments.

solution.label: a
steps: The distance from O is multiplied by 3, and the point turns through \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) anticlockwise about O.
solution.answer: \(6e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}\): an enlargement by 3 and a rotation of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)

stem: A survey drone starts at the origin O of an Argand diagram, where the real axis points east, the imaginary axis points north and distances are in metres. It flies three straight legs, given as complex numbers: \[120e^{0.5i}, \quad 80e^{2.1i}, \quad 60e^{-1.0i}.\] Arguments are in radians, measured anticlockwise from east.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the first leg in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the position of the drone after the three legs, in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance of the drone from O, and the argument of its position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The drone flies straight back to O. Write this return leg in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), where \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).

idea: Displacements add like complex numbers: write each leg in Cartesian form, add, then turn the total back into modulus and argument. The return leg is the negative of the total.

solution.label: b
steps: Second leg: \(-40.38\ldots + 69.05\ldots i\). Third leg: \(32.41\ldots - 50.48\ldots i\).

stem: Two loudspeakers play the same note. At a listener's position, the pressure changes from the two speakers are modelled by \(p_{1} = 4\sin(300t)\) and \(p_{2} = 3\sin(300t + \varphi)\), where \(t\) is in seconds and angles are in radians. The combined sound is \(p_{1} + p_{2} = A\sin(300t + \alpha)\), where \(A\) and \(\alpha\) are found from the complex number \(4 + 3e^{i\varphi} = Ae^{i\alpha}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For \(\varphi = 1.2\), find \(A\) and \(\alpha\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(\varphi\), with \(0 < \varphi < \pi\), for which \(A = 5\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For \(0 \le \varphi \le \pi\), write down the least possible value of \(A\), and the value of \(\varphi\) that gives it.

idea: Sinusoids with the same frequency add like complex numbers (phasors): add \(4e^{0i}\) and \(3e^{i\varphi}\), then the modulus is the new amplitude and the argument is the new phase.

solution.label: c
steps: \(A^{2} = 25 + 24\cos\varphi\) is least when \(\cos\varphi = -1\): \(A^{2} = 1\). The two waves are exactly out of step.

stem: In an alternating current circuit, each component has a complex impedance \(Z\) ohms. Two components in series have total impedance \(Z_{1} + Z_{2}\); two in parallel have total impedance \(\dfrac{Z_{1}Z_{2}}{Z_{1} + Z_{2}}\). The size of the current, in amps, is \(\dfrac{230}{|Z|}\) for a 230 volt supply, and the phase angle is \(\arg Z\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The components are connected in series. Find the total impedance, its modulus, and the size of the current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The components are connected in parallel. Find the total impedance in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the parallel circuit, find the size of the current and the phase angle, in radians.

idea: Combine the impedances with complex arithmetic: add for series; multiply, add and divide for parallel, using the conjugate to divide. Then the modulus and argument give the size of the current and the phase angle.

stem: A point moves on an Argand diagram in jumps. It starts at \(z_{0} = 10\), and each jump takes it from \(z_{n}\) to \(z_{n + 1} = 0.9e^{\frac{\pi}{4}i}z_{n}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(z_{1}\) in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(z_{8}\) is a positive real number, and find it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the smallest value of \(n\) for which \(|z_{n}| < 1\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Each jump is a straight line from \(z_{n}\) to \(z_{n + 1}\). Find the total length of all the jumps if the point jumps for ever.

idea: Each jump multiplies by \(0.9e^{\frac{\pi}{4}i}\): it shrinks the distance from O by 0.9 and turns through \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). So \(z_{n} = 10(0.9)^{n}e^{\frac{n\pi}{4}i}\), and the lengths of the jumps form a geometric series.

stem: Let \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{B} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(\boldsymbol{A} + \boldsymbol{B}\) and \(2\boldsymbol{A} - \boldsymbol{B}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\boldsymbol{AB}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(\det \boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\).

idea: Add and subtract matrices entry by entry. In a product, each entry is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second. For \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\), the determinant is \(ad - bc\) and the inverse is \(\dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}\).

stem: The matrix \(\boldsymbol{N}\) gives the grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat (columns in that order) in one portion of oats, milk and banana (rows in that order). The matrix \(\boldsymbol{Q}\) gives the number of portions of each food in a breakfast (top row) and in a snack (bottom row).
\[\boldsymbol{N} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 27 & 3 \\ 8 & 12 & 5 \\ 1 & 27 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{Q} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the order of the matrix \(\boldsymbol{QN}\), and explain why \(\boldsymbol{NQ}\) does not exist.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\boldsymbol{QN}\), and state what its top row shows.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Protein and carbohydrate give 4 kcal per gram and fat gives 9 kcal per gram. Use a matrix product to find the energy in the breakfast and in the snack.

idea: A product \(\boldsymbol{QN}\) exists when the number of columns of \(\boldsymbol{Q}\) equals the number of rows of \(\boldsymbol{N}\); it then has the rows of \(\boldsymbol{Q}\) and the columns of \(\boldsymbol{N}\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(\boldsymbol{Q}\) is \(2 \times 3\) and \(\boldsymbol{N}\) is \(3 \times 3\), so \(\boldsymbol{QN}\) is \(2 \times 3\). For \(\boldsymbol{NQ}\), \(\boldsymbol{N}\) has 3 columns but \(\boldsymbol{Q}\) has only 2 rows.
solution.answer: \(2 \times 3\); the sizes do not match for \(\boldsymbol{NQ}\)

solution.label: b
solution.answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}19 & 93 & 11 \\ 10 & 66 & 5\end{pmatrix}\); the top row is the grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat in the breakfast

stem: A jeweller has three alloys. Alloy X is 60 % gold, 30 % silver and 10 % copper; alloy Y is 40 % gold, 40 % silver and 20 % copper; alloy Z is 10 % gold, 20 % silver and 70 % copper. She melts together \(x\) grams of X, \(y\) grams of Y and \(z\) grams of Z to make a mixture with 40.5 g of gold, 31 g of silver and 28.5 g of copper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a system of three linear equations, and write it as a matrix equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The jeweller wants a 50 g piece with the same make-up. Find the mass of each alloy she needs.

idea: Each metal gives one equation. The system \(\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{c}\) has the unique solution \(\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{c}\) when \(\det \boldsymbol{M} \ne 0\).

solution.label: c
steps: The mixture above has mass \(40 + 35 + 25 = 100\) g, so halve each mass.
solution.answer: 20 g of X, 17.5 g of Y and 12.5 g of Z

stem: Let \(\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{pmatrix}k & 2 \\ 3 & k - 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(k \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the values of \(k\) for which \(\boldsymbol{M}\) has no inverse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For \(k = 1\), use \(\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\) to solve \(\boldsymbol{M}\begin{pmatrix}x \\ y\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}\).

idea: A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero.

stem: Let \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{I}\) be the \(2 \times 2\) identity matrix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(\boldsymbol{A}^{2}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of \(p\) and \(q\) such that \(\boldsymbol{A}^{2} = p\boldsymbol{A} + q\boldsymbol{I}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence show that \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{4}(5\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{A})\), and check your answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the result of part (b) to find \(\boldsymbol{A}^{3}\) without multiplying three matrices.

idea: Compare the matrices entry by entry to find \(p\) and \(q\). Multiplying the equation by \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) gives the inverse; multiplying it by \(\boldsymbol{A}\) gives \(\boldsymbol{A}^{3}\) in terms of \(\boldsymbol{A}^{2}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(p\boldsymbol{A} + q\boldsymbol{I} = \begin{pmatrix}3p + q & p \\ 2p & 2p + q\end{pmatrix}\). Top right: \(p = 5\). Top left: \(15 + q = 11\).

stem: A bakery makes batches of three products, P, Q and R, using three machines. The matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\) gives the hours each machine (rows 1 to 3) spends on one batch of each product (columns P, Q, R). In one day the machines are used for 20, 19 and 27 hours.
\[\boldsymbol{T} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a matrix equation for the numbers of batches \(p\), \(q\) and \(r\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\det \boldsymbol{T}\), and explain what it tells you about the solution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the numbers of batches.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Machine 1 can be used for 2 more hours. Find the change in the numbers of batches, using \(\boldsymbol{T}^{-1}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Comment on your answer to part (d).

idea: \(\boldsymbol{T}\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{h}\), so \(\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{T}^{-1}\boldsymbol{h}\). Because the system is linear, a change \(\Delta\boldsymbol{h}\) in the hours changes the batches by \(\boldsymbol{T}^{-1}\Delta\boldsymbol{h}\).

solution.label: a
steps: Each row: hours used on that machine.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: \(-7 \ne 0\), so \(\boldsymbol{T}^{-1}\) exists and there is exactly one solution

solution.label: e
steps: Using all the extra time on machine 1 means making more Q and less P and R, and the changes are not whole batches.
solution.answer: In practice the bakery cannot make part batches, so it would round, and not every machine would be fully used

stem: Let \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the characteristic polynomial of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and hence its eigenvalues.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.

idea: The eigenvalues \(\lambda\) solve \(\det(\boldsymbol{A} - \lambda\boldsymbol{I}) = 0\). An eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) for \(\lambda\) is any non-zero solution of \((\boldsymbol{A} - \lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}\).

stem: The matrix \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues 5 and 2, with eigenvectors \(\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down matrices \(\boldsymbol{P}\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}\), where \(\boldsymbol{D}\) is diagonal, such that \(\boldsymbol{A} = \boldsymbol{PDP}^{-1}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find \(\boldsymbol{A}^{5}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the sum of the eigenvalues equals the sum of the diagonal entries of \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

idea: Put the eigenvectors in the columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) and the eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{D}\). Then \(\boldsymbol{A}^{n} = \boldsymbol{PD}^{n}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\), and \(\boldsymbol{D}^{n}\) just raises each diagonal entry to the power \(n\).

solution.label: a
steps: Columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\): the eigenvectors for 5 and for 2.

stem: A town has 120 hire bikes, kept at two docking stations, North and South. Each day, 80 % of the bikes that start at North end the day at North and 20 % end at South; 70 % of those that start at South stay there and 30 % end at North. On Monday morning there are 70 bikes at North and 50 at South.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\), with columns for the starting station.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the expected number of bikes at each station after 3 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the long-term number of bikes at each station, and explain your method.

idea: Each column of a transition matrix shows where the bikes from one station go, so each column adds up to 1. The state after \(n\) days is \(\boldsymbol{T}^{n}\boldsymbol{s}_{0}\), and the long-term state is the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1, scaled to the total.

solution.label: a
steps: Column 1: from North; column 2: from South.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: About 71.75 bikes at North and 48.25 at South

solution.label: c
steps: The long-term state \(\boldsymbol{s}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{Ts} = \boldsymbol{s}\): an eigenvector for eigenvalue 1. From \(0.8n + 0.3s = n\): \(0.2n = 0.3s\), so \(n : s = 3 : 2\).

stem: A simple weather model has two states, sunny and rainy. If a day is sunny, the next day is sunny with probability 0.7; if a day is rainy, the next day is sunny with probability 0.4. The transition matrix, with columns for today's weather (sunny, rainy), is \(\boldsymbol{T} = \begin{pmatrix}0.7 & 0.4 \\ 0.3 & 0.6\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{T}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Day 0 is sunny. Use \(\boldsymbol{T} = \boldsymbol{PDP}^{-1}\) to show that the probability that day \(n\) is sunny is \(\dfrac{4}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7}(0.3)^{n}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the probability that day 2 is sunny, and the long-term proportion of sunny days.

idea: Every transition matrix has 1 as an eigenvalue; its eigenvector gives the long-term state. Writing the starting state in terms of the eigenvectors shows how the other part dies away as \((0.3)^{n}\).

stem: A town library has three branches, A, B and C. Each week, a borrowed book is returned to a branch as follows.

Of the books borrowed from A, 70 % are returned to A, 20 % to B and 10 % to C. Of those borrowed from B, 15 % go to A, 75 % to B and 10 % to C. Of those borrowed from C, 10 % go to A, 20 % to B and 70 % to C. Assume every book is borrowed and returned once a week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\), with columns for the branch a book is borrowed from (A, B, C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A book starts at branch B. Find the probability that it is at branch A after two weeks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the long-term proportion of books at each branch.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The library has 720 books. Find the long-term number at each branch.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The other two eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{T}\) are 0.6 and 0.55. Explain what this tells you about how quickly the numbers settle.

idea: The probabilities after two weeks are in \(\boldsymbol{T}^{2}\). The long-term proportions form the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1, scaled so that its entries add to 1. The other eigenvalues control how fast the differences die away.

solution.label: b
steps: The entry in row A, column B of \(\boldsymbol{T}^{2}\): \(0.7 \times 0.15 + 0.15 \times 0.75 + 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.105 + 0.1125 + 0.01\)

solution.label: e
steps: The distance from the long-term state shrinks roughly by a factor of 0.6 each week, so after 10 weeks it is about \(0.6^{10} \approx 0.006\) of what it was.
solution.answer: The numbers settle quickly, within a few weeks
